newsitem.title: USA: Industry hits at U.S. Treasury rules for non-banks.
newsitem.headline: Industry hits at U.S. Treasury rules for non-banks.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury proposal to counter money laundering at non-bank financial institutions would be costly for the industry and the government, industry representatives told a House committee Wednesday.
The Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) plans to bring money services businesses (MSBs) -- such as wire transfer agencies and check cashers -- under Federal supervision.
But MSBs vary widely in the kinds financial services they provide and in the size of their operations, making umbrella regulation difficult, members of the industry told a House Banking subcommittee.

Jerome Gagerman, speaking for the National Check Cashers Association, testified certain FinCEN proposals are prejudicial. The suggestion that only businesses primarily engaged in financial services be required to register with the Treasury would create unfair competition, he said.
"Numerous businesses cash checks in direct competition with us, including liquor stores, groceries and convenience stores," said Gagerman, who is also president of Financial Clearings Inc.
"While we must train our employees and develop compliance plans, our major competitors would be exempt from such activities," he said.
Another industry group testified that some businesses should be exempt from FinCEN's proposed rules.
Mark Plotkin, counsel for consortium Mondex USA, said Treasury's plan would discourage the development of stored-value technology, a sort of electronic currency.
Requiring all firms involved in money services to register as MSBs, for example, would dissuade potential Mondex licensees, Plotkin said.
"The regulatory requirements that FinCEN has proposed are, at present, quite premature," he said.
Some of FinCEN's other requirements seem arbitrary and inefficient, said Ezra Levine, testifying on behalf of money transmitters such as Western Union and American Express.
Particularly troubling were requirements that "suspicious" transactions exceeding $500 or any transfer of more than $750 outside the United States be reported, Levine said.

"The threshold is too low ... and would result in the countless filing of inestimable numbers of useless SARs (Suspicious Activity Reports) at major expense to industry with questionable benefit to law enforcement," he said.
Processing the report proposed for foreign transfers would cost the industry more than $11 million a year, Levine projected.
Stanley Morris, director of FinCEN, said the $750 figure arose from a successful counter-money laundering operation in New York.
Morris added, however, that FinCEN would study the MSB industry closely and might be willing to alter reporting rules in the future.
The Treasury expects to finalize its MSB regulations by the end of September, with the rules going into effect by July 1, 1998, Morris said.
